justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple motor-vehicle lanes, while pedestrian space is visually limited to narrow side sidewalks, indicating an uneven distribution of public right-of-way.

A planted median and side planting strips provide some environmental benefits for all users, but these landscape resources are concentrated between carriageways rather than clearly supporting sidewalk use.
Sidewalks appear continuous along both sides of the road, which supports basic access, but no visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossings can be confirmed from the image.
There is no visible dedicated cycling facility despite the road width, suggesting that space is not fairly distributed to cyclists compared with drivers.
safety: The roadway is wide, with clear lane markings and a landscaped median, which helps organize traffic and reduce head-on conflict.
Traffic volume is very low in the image, with only one visible van ahead, which lowers immediate crash risk and perceived stress for current road users.
Streetlights are present along the corridor, supporting baseline visibility and nighttime traffic safety.
However, the broad carriageway encourages higher vehicle speeds, and no visible pedestrian crossing, refuge island access point, or traffic-calming feature is present.
livability: The corridor feels low in street life because there are no visible pedestrians, storefronts, cafes, or active ground-floor uses along the road edge.
Large construction cranes, green construction fencing, and scaffold structures on the right side indicate an unfinished or transitional urban environment rather than a settled neighborhood street.
The road appears designed mainly for through-movement of vehicles, with limited visible amenities such as benches, bus stops, or gathering spaces.
Some trees and planted medians improve environmental quality, but they do not compensate for the lack of visible daily-use destinations and social activity.
sustainability: The central and roadside planting strips with trees and shrubs add urban greenery and can contribute to air-quality improvement and stormwater moderation.
The orderly boulevard form and long, straight corridor could support efficient transit or future multimodal travel, but no visible bus stop or transit priority feature is evident in this frame.
There is no visible protected bike lane or bicycle parking, which weakens support for low-carbon active transport.
The street devotes a large share of space to motor traffic lanes, indicating a car-oriented layout with limited current support for mode shift.
aesthetics: The road has a clean and orderly appearance, with fresh pavement, crisp lane markings, and regularly spaced streetlights.
Trees and low shrubs in the median and roadside strips soften the corridor and add some visual rhythm.
At the same time, the sky is visually dominant and the corridor feels somewhat empty and monotonous because of the long straight alignment and sparse edge activity.
Construction cranes, scaffold frames, and green site fencing reduce visual refinement and make the streetscape feel incomplete.
comfort: Thermal comfort is moderate to low because trees are present but provide limited canopy shade over the sidewalks and roadway.

Physical comfort for drivers is relatively good due to the smooth pavement and wide lanes, but comfort for pedestrians is less certain because the sidewalk zone appears exposed and minimally furnished.
Psychological comfort is mixed: low traffic reduces immediate stress, yet the oversized road width and lack of visible human activity can make the space feel isolated.
No benches, shelters, or other resting amenities are visible, which lowers overall comfort for non-motorized users.
walkability: Sidewalks appear to exist on both sides of the street, which supports basic pedestrian continuity.
Walkability is weakened by the very wide roadway and the absence of any visible marked crosswalk or pedestrian crossing opportunity in the image.
The street edge lacks active frontage, shops, or visible entrances, so there are few cues that would attract or sustain walking trips.
Limited sidewalk shade and a generally exposed environment reduce walking comfort, especially over long distances.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, buffered cycle track, or bicycle symbols are visible despite the generous roadway width.
The wide, straight multi-lane carriageway may encourage faster motor traffic, which increases stress for cyclists riding in mixed traffic.
There is no visible bicycle parking, bike signal, or intersection treatment supporting cycling convenience or safety.
Landscaped medians and clear lane organization improve general order, but they do not substitute for protected cycling infrastructure.
